items.q: A Python script that cleans a 1 GB CSV in 3 minutes now has to handle 100 GB every night. What breaks first, and what do you change?
points: Memory: reading the whole file at once fails; stream it in chunks or with generators
A single core becomes the limit; move the heavy work to DuckDB, Polars or Spark instead of adding threads
The runtime passes the nightly window; partition the input so parts run in parallel and can be retried alone
Name the point where you would stop scaling the script and move to an engine

items.q: Your nightly Spark job runs for 2 hours on 1 TB. Data grows 100× over two years. What breaks first, and what is your plan?
points: Shuffle and skew grow faster than data: the widest join or aggregation breaks first
Full reprocessing stops fitting the window: move to incremental processing by partition
Small files and metadata growth slow the table; compaction and partition design matter
Cost grows with it: state the cost per run now and at 100×
Say what you would measure before changing anything

items.q: A Kafka topic carries 5,000 events a second today. Product wants 500,000. What breaks, in order?
points: Partition count caps consumer parallelism; adding partitions later reshuffles keys and order
Consumer lag and rebalances; state size in the stream processor
Broker disk and network; retention times throughput
Hot keys: one big city or merchant overloads one partition
Downstream sinks often break before Kafka does

items.q: A star schema serves 20 analysts well. The company grows to 2,000 users and 40 teams querying it. What breaks?
points: Concurrency and cost on the warehouse; workload isolation and caching
Conflicting metric definitions as teams add their own; a semantic layer or shared metrics
Wide fact tables and slowly changing dimensions grow; partition and cluster for the common filters
Ownership: who approves changes to shared dimensions

items.q: An LLM-based assistant answers 50 questions a day for one team. It is rolled out to 5,000 employees. What breaks?
points: Cost and rate limits; caching, smaller models for easy questions, budgets per team
Quality drift across many more question types; evals that grow with real questions
Access control: users must only retrieve what they are allowed to see
Latency and observability: tracing each answer to its sources

items.q: At 3 a.m. the nightly Python ingestion job is killed for using too much memory. It worked yesterday. Walk me through the first 15 minutes.
points: Stop the damage: is anything downstream reading partial data? Pause or mark the run failed clearly
Compare inputs: did today's file grow, change shape, or contain one giant record?
Check the last code or dependency change
Rerun safely only if the job is idempotent; otherwise fix the partial output first
Write down the follow-up: streaming the input and an alert on input size

items.q: The revenue dashboard shows yesterday's revenue doubled. The CFO has already seen it. Walk me through the first 15 minutes.
points: Assume a data problem until proven otherwise; tell stakeholders it is being checked, with a time for the next update
Check freshness and row counts by source and partition: duplicates from a rerun are the most common cause
Trace lineage from the dashboard back to the first table where the number is wrong
Fix forward or roll back the bad partition; then add the check that would have caught it (a uniqueness or volume test)

items.q: Consumer lag on the payments topic has grown for an hour and real-time fraud scores are 40 minutes late. What do you do?
points: Find whether input rose or processing slowed: compare produce rate and consume rate
Look for a poison message, a slow sink, a rebalance loop or one hot partition
Short term: scale consumers up to the partition count, skip to a dead-letter queue, or degrade to batch scoring
Communicate the business impact (fraud checks are late), then the fix and the follow-up

items.q: Your on-call agent posted a wrong root cause for a pipeline failure in the incident channel, and an engineer acted on it. What now?
points: Correct it in the channel first and stop the wrong action
Find why: missing evidence, a tool returning stale data, or the model guessing
Add an eval case from this incident; require the agent to cite evidence for each claim
Decide what the agent may do alone and what needs a human approval

items.q: For a 50 GB daily job, pick pandas, Polars, DuckDB or Spark, and say what you rejected and why.
points: Name the decision drivers: data size, team skills, where it runs, cost
A single-node engine (DuckDB or Polars) often wins at 50 GB on one machine: no cluster to run
Reject pandas for memory, and Spark for operational cost unless data or concurrency grows a lot
State the condition that would change your choice

items.q: The team wants Kafka for 200 events a minute from one service to one consumer. Approve or push back?
points: Push back unless replay, many consumers or ordering per key are needed soon
A queue (SQS) or a table with a poller is cheaper to run at this volume
Kafka's cost is operations: brokers, upgrades, schema registry, on-call
Say what future need would make Kafka the right call, and how to switch later

items.q: Iceberg, Delta Lake or Hudi for a new lakehouse used by Spark, Trino and Snowflake. Pick one and defend it.
points: Engine support decides first: which engines must read and write
Iceberg is the most engine-neutral; Delta is strongest inside Databricks; Hudi fits heavy upserts
Name what you give up with your pick
Mention catalog choice, because it matters as much as the table format

items.q: One big wide table or a star schema for the company's core business metrics? Defend your choice.
points: Star schema: one place to change a dimension, history kept, shared by many tables
Wide table: fast and simple for one use case, but duplicated logic and painful history
Often both: star as the source of truth, wide tables built from it for dashboards
Say who maintains each and what it costs to change

items.q: Databricks or Snowflake as the main platform for a 300-person company? You must pick one.
points: Start from the workloads: SQL analytics, data science, streaming, AI
Snowflake: less to operate, strong SQL and governance; Databricks: stronger for Spark, ML and open formats
Cost model and skills of the current team
State how you would keep the exit door open (open table formats)

items.q: Leadership asks whether the new in-app coaching feature is working. Define the metric, then the table that would compute it.
points: One north-star metric tied to the goal (for example, share of users who complete a practice session in week 2), plus guardrails
Define the grain: one row per user per day, or one row per session
Name the events needed and how late or duplicate events are handled
Say how you would avoid fooling yourself: a comparison group or a before-after with care

items.q: How would you know if shared rides (pooling) is working? Define the metrics, then model the fact table.
points: Metrics for riders (wait and trip time), drivers (earnings per hour) and the business (cost per trip), with one north star
Grain: one row per ride segment or per pooled trip, and why
Dimensions: rider, driver, zone, time; handle a trip whose riders change mid-route
Guardrails: cancellation rate and rider rating

items.q: Daily active users dropped 15% overnight. How do you find out whether it is real or a data problem?
points: Check data first: late or missing events by platform, app version and region
Compare with an independent source (logins, server logs)
If real, slice by segment to find where the drop sits
Report what you know, what you do not yet know, and when you will know

items.q: Forty pipelines across six teams produce three different revenue numbers. What is your plan for the next two quarters?
points: First month: inventory the pipelines and owners, and agree one definition of revenue with finance
Build one certified revenue table with tests and an owner; deprecate the others on a dated plan
Make the right way the easy way: a template and a metrics layer, not a policy document
Measure progress: number of certified metrics, number of retired pipelines, incidents

items.q: You join as the first data architect at a 500-person company with no data platform strategy. What do you do in your first 90 days?
points: Listen first: meet the main data consumers and producers, and list their top pains
Write a short current-state map and three to five principles
Pick one visible win in the first quarter
Deliver a strategy document with a roadmap, costs and what you will not do

items.q: Every team writes its pipelines in a different style and Python version, and on-call is painful. How do you fix that without slowing teams down?
points: A golden path: a template repo with the Python version, packaging, tests, logging and CI already set up
Make it the fastest way to start, not a mandate
Migrate the worst offenders first, measured by incidents
Keep an exception process for real needs

items.q: Cut the data platform bill by 40% this quarter without missing any service level. Where do you look first?
points: Measure first: cost by team, job and table (tagging and showback)
Biggest wins are usually idle clusters, oversized warehouses, full refreshes that could be incremental, and unused tables
Storage tiering and retention for old raw data
Agree with each team what service level it really needs

items.q: Your LLM features cost 30,000 dollars a month and finance wants it halved. What do you do?
points: Measure cost by feature and prompt
Cache repeated work, shorten prompts and context, route easy requests to smaller models
Batch offline work, cap tokens per request, set budgets per team
Check that quality does not drop with evals before and after

items.q: Warehouse costs doubled in six months while data grew 20%. What is going on, and what do you change?
points: Find the top queries and jobs by cost: often dashboards refreshing too often or full rebuilds
Clustering, materialised aggregates, and incremental models
Workload isolation and auto-suspend
Make cost visible to the teams who create it

items.q: Move the orders data from Postgres to a lakehouse with no downtime, and prove nothing was lost.
points: Initial snapshot plus change data capture from the same log position
Run both in parallel; reconcile counts and sums per day and per key
Switch readers one by one with a rollback plan
Decide when the old path is turned off, and who signs off

items.q: Migrate 300 Hive jobs to Spark on a lakehouse in the cloud over a year. How do you plan it?
points: Inventory and group the jobs by pattern; automate the common patterns
Migrate by business domain with a parallel run and automated comparison
Freeze new development on the old platform with a date
Track progress and cost every month; keep the team who owns each job involved

items.q: A critical pipeline is a 4,000-line Python script nobody wants to touch. How do you replace it safely?
points: Characterisation tests: capture its outputs on real inputs first
Strangle it: move one part at a time behind the same interface
Run old and new side by side and compare outputs
Remove the old part only when the comparison has been clean for a while

items.q: 2 million ride events a minute, 1 KB each. How many Kafka partitions, and how much storage a day with 7 days of retention and replication 3?
points: About 33,000 events a second, about 33 MB a second
At around 5 to 10 MB a second per partition consumer, roughly 8 to 16 partitions, more for headroom and peaks
About 2.9 TB a day raw; times 3 replicas and 7 days is about 60 TB
State the assumptions out loud and round

items.q: How much memory does a Python dict with 50 million string keys and integer values need? Would you hold it in memory?
points: Each entry costs the key string object, the int object and the hash table slot: roughly 100 bytes or more per entry
So about 5 GB or more: too big for many workers
Alternatives: a sorted array, a database, DuckDB, or processing by partition
Say how you would measure it (tracemalloc) instead of guessing

items.q: A fact table gets 500 million rows a day at 200 bytes a row in Parquet. How big is a year, and how would you partition it?
points: About 100 GB a day uncompressed, maybe 20 to 30 GB compressed; around 10 TB a year compressed
Partition by day (or hour if queries are hourly); avoid partitions smaller than about 1 GB
Cluster by the common filter columns
Plan retention and compaction

items.q: Walk me through the most complex data system you built: why each main choice, what failed, and what you would change now.
points: A one-minute overview: the business problem, scale and your role
Two or three key decisions with the alternatives you rejected
One real failure and what you changed afterwards
What you would do differently today, and the measurable impact

items.q: Tell me about a design decision you got wrong. How did you find out, and what did you do?
points: Pick a real decision with consequences
How you detected it (metrics, incidents, user feedback)
How you fixed it and communicated it
What you do differently now

items.q: Another team's design will hurt your platform, and you do not manage them. What do you do?
points: Understand their goals and constraints first
Bring data: the cost or risk to your platform, in their terms
Offer an alternative that meets their goal, and agree a decision maker
Disagree and commit if the decision goes against you, with the risk written down

items.q: A senior engineer on your team keeps shipping pipelines without tests and says they slow him down. How do you handle it?
points: Talk one to one about outcomes: incidents and rework, not rules
Make testing cheap: templates and examples
Agree a clear standard for the team, applied to everyone
Follow up and recognise the change

items.q: You must say no to a VP who wants a real-time dashboard by next week. How do you handle it?
points: Ask what decision the dashboard supports and how fresh the data truly needs to be
Offer options with dates: hourly next week, real time in a quarter
Be clear about the cost and risk of rushing
Confirm the agreement in writing

items.q: Design a payments-style write API that is safe to retry. What exactly makes it idempotent?
points: The client sends an idempotency key with each request
The server stores the key and the result in the same transaction as the write; a repeated key returns the stored result
Keys expire after a window; a unique constraint backs it up
Say what happens if two requests with the same key arrive at the same moment (a lock or insert-first on the key)

items.q: Backfill a new column on a two-billion-row table that takes writes all day, without hurting production.
points: Expand, write to both (CDC or a trigger), backfill, verify, switch reads, contract
Small primary-key batches, each committed, resumable from the last id, idempotent
Throttle on replication lag and load; never one giant transaction or OFFSET paging
Rollback stays possible until the old structure is dropped

items.q: A metrics API in front of the warehouse serves 50 requests a second. A new app launch will bring 5,000. What do you put in front of it?
points: A cache with invalidation on data refresh and a time-to-live; protect against a thundering herd
Precomputed aggregates for the common queries
Rate limits per client and a circuit breaker in front of the warehouse
Horizontal API servers behind a load balancer; say what the warehouse itself can take

items.q: Design surge pricing for one city: estimate the event rate and state size, then say how you would flag drivers behaving oddly.
points: Estimate drivers and riders online, location pings per second and zones; state per zone is small
A streaming job aggregates supply and demand per zone per minute; price comes from the ratio, smoothed
Anomalies: compare each driver with recent fare-per-km and acceptance baselines; beware drivers who just lost network
Say what runs in real time and what runs in batch, and how you would test it
